package.script: Ever wonder why your soda can feels ready to pop when you are flying high above the clouds? Here is the thing, it is all about invisible air pressure pushing from both the inside and the outside. Down on the ground, thick air pushes hard against the metal aluminum walls to keep everything stable. But as you climb way up into the sky, the surrounding air gets much thinner and weaker. Suddenly, the trapped gas bubbles inside your drink start expanding like crazy because they have no resistance. The metal stretches, the top bulges outward, and honestly, it is just waiting for a tiny crack to burst open. That is why opening a warm soda after a flight always turns into a sticky surprise. Would you dare open a shaken can at thirty thousand feet, or would you just hand it back?

package.description:
The weirdest ways animals sleep: sea otters holding paws, birds that nap mid-flight and elephants sleeping standing up. Here are 5 animals with the strangest sleep habits, counted down to number one.

In this Short: sea otters, sperm whales, the common swift, frigatebirds and wild African elephants, and how each one gets its rest.

scenes.text: You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these five animals do it. We're counting down to the strangest sleeper on the planet.

scenes.text: Number five: sea otters. They float on their backs and often hold paws, so they don't drift apart.

stock_queries: two sea otters holding paws water
scenes.image_prompt: Two sea otters floating peacefully on their backs in clear blue ocean water holding paws, sunlight glinting on wet fur, National Geographic wildlife photography style.

scenes.text: Number four: sperm whales. They nap upright, like giant floating pillars, for just ten to fifteen minutes.
scenes.label: Sperm Whales
stock_queries: pod of whales drifting upright underwater
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater wide shot of massive sperm whales sleeping suspended vertically in crystal clear deep ocean waters, sun rays piercing through the surface, eerie and serene nature photography.

scenes.text: Number three: the common swift. This bird can stay airborne for about ten months straight, and scientists think it naps up there.

Common myths debunked in a quick true-or-false quiz: the goldfish 3-second memory, seeing the Great Wall of China from space, and bulls hating red. How many did you get right?

In this Short: three school 'facts', a 3-second countdown for each, and what the science actually says.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/goldfish-memory.html
https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/can-you-see-great-wall-china-from-space
https://wonderopolis.org/wonder/do-bulls-hate-the-color-red
tags: great wall of china visible from space
great wall of china seen from space
package.pinned_comment: Bonus: astronauts say that from orbit, city lights and big highways are far easier to spot than the Great Wall. Which of these myths fooled you the longest?

scenes.text: Three facts you probably still believe, and you have three seconds to guess which are false. Say true or false out loud before the timer runs out.
scenes.label: 3 School Facts
stock_queries: student raising hand in a classroom
scenes.image_prompt: A modern classroom with a student raising their hand, bright cinematic lighting, 4k resolution
scenes.stock_query: student raising hand in a classroom

scenes.text: Fact one: goldfish only remember things for three seconds. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Goldfish Memory
scenes.image_prompt: A close-up shot of an orange goldfish swimming in a clean glass bowl with green plants

scenes.text: False! Scientists have trained goldfish to respond to sounds and remember them for months.
scenes.label: False: Months!
stock_queries: goldfish swimming toward a person hand
scenes.image_prompt: A goldfish swimming near the edge of a glass bowl, macro photography, vivid orange color
scenes.stock_query: goldfish swimming toward a person hand

scenes.text: Fact two: you can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Great Wall From Space
stock_queries: great wall of china winding over hills
scenes.image_prompt: An aerial view of the Great Wall of China winding across green mountain ridges at sunset
scenes.stock_query: great wall of china winding over hills

scenes.text: False again! From orbit it's very hard to spot, because it's narrow and the same color as the land around it.
scenes.label: False: Too Narrow
stock_queries: earth seen from space at night
scenes.image_prompt: Planet Earth viewed from space showing continents and atmosphere, cinematic style
scenes.stock_query: earth seen from space at night

scenes.text: Fact three: bulls get angry when they see the color red. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Bulls Hate Red
scenes.image_prompt: A strong black bull standing in a green grassy field, natural daylight

scenes.text: Also false! Bulls can't see red the way you do. It's the cape's movement that gets their attention.
scenes.label: False: Movement
stock_queries: cattle walking and moving in a field
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a bull looking directly at the camera in a sunny pasture
scenes.stock_query: cattle walking and moving in a field

scenes.text: So the answer: all three are false. How many did you get right? Zero, one, two or three? Be honest in the comments. Here's another round: three facts you probably still believe…
scenes.label: What's Your Score?
stock_queries: student raising hand in a classroom
scenes.image_prompt: A person holding up fingers to count, clean studio background, bright lighting

key_facts: Goldfish can remember things for months, not just three seconds.
The Great Wall of China is very difficult to see from space with the naked eye because it is narrow and blends with the landscape.
Bulls cannot see red the way humans do; they react to the movement of the cape rather than its color.
package.script: Three facts you probably still believe, and you have three seconds to guess which are false. Say true or false out loud before the timer runs out. Fact one: goldfish only remember things for three seconds. Three, two, one. False! Scientists have trained goldfish to respond to sounds and remember them for months. Fact two: you can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes. Three, two, one. False again! From orbit it's very hard to spot, because it's narrow and the same color as the land around it. Fact three: bulls get angry when they see the color red. Three, two, one. Also false! Bulls can't see red the way you do. It's the cape's movement that gets their attention. So the answer: all three are false. How many did you get right? Zero, one, two or three? Be honest in the comments. Here's another round: three facts you probably still believe…

package.title: Top 5 Peppers That Make Jalapeños Look Mild
package.description:
The hottest peppers in the world ranked by Scoville heat, from the habanero to Pepper X, the hottest pepper in the world according to Guinness. Admire them, don't eat them!

In this Short: habanero, ghost pepper, Trinidad Moruga Scorpion, Carolina Reaper and Pepper X, compared with a jalapeño.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hottest_chili_pepper
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepper_X
https://accuweather.com/en/weather-news/guinness-world-records-declares-pepper-x-as-worlds-new-hottest-chili-pepper/1588288
tags: hottest pepper in the world pepper x
hottest pepper in the world comparison
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: chili heat comes from a chemical called capsaicin, and birds barely feel it at all, which helps them spread pepper seeds. Hottest thing you've ever tried?

scenes.text: You think jalapeños are hot? The pepper at number one is hundreds of times hotter. Let's count down five peppers that make a jalapeño look mild. Pepper heat is measured in Scoville units, and a jalapeño is only a few thousand.
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic vertical macro shot of fresh glossy green jalapeño peppers on a dark rustic wooden cutting board, soft studio lighting, ultra-realistic food photography, 9:16 aspect ratio

scenes.text: Number five: the habanero. Up to around three hundred fifty thousand. Already way too much for most people.
scenes.label: Habanero
scenes.image_prompt: Vibrant vertical close-up of glossy bright orange habanero peppers grouped together on a dark textured slate background, dramatic warm lighting, 8k resolution, 9:16 aspect ratio

scenes.text: Number four: the ghost pepper. Around one million. It was the first pepper ever measured over a million.
scenes.label: Ghost Pepper
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical macro photography of wrinkled red Bhut Jolokia ghost peppers lying on dark charred wood, subtle smoky atmosphere, cinematic shallow depth of field, 9:16 aspect ratio

scenes.text: Number three: the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. Around one point two million, with a little stinger-like tail.
scenes.label: Trinidad Moruga Scorpion
scenes.image_prompt: Detailed vertical extreme close-up of a deep crimson Trinidad Moruga Scorpion chili pepper showing textured bumpy skin and pointed stinger tail, dark moody lighting, 9:16 aspect ratio

scenes.text: Number two: the Carolina Reaper. About one point six million. It held the world record for about ten years.
scenes.label: Carolina Reaper
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical dramatic shot of a gnarly bright red Carolina Reaper chili pepper with its signature tail, perched against a dark stone surface with faint rising heat haze, 9:16 aspect ratio

scenes.text: Number one: Pepper X. About two point seven million. That's the hottest pepper in the world, according to Guinness.
scenes.label: Pepper X
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical macro shot of a heavily wrinkled greenish-yellow superhot pepper glowing under intense studio rim light against a pitch-black background, ultra detailed texture, 9:16 aspect ratio

scenes.text: Please, admire these with your eyes, not your mouth. What's the hottest thing you've ever eaten? Tell me below. And if you think jalapeños are hot…
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical cinematic shot of a person desperately holding a cold glass of milk with condensation, sitting at a wooden kitchen counter, humorous culinary scene, 9:16 aspect ratio

key_facts: Pepper heat is measured in Scoville heat units (SHU).
A standard jalapeño pepper measures only a few thousand Scoville units.
The habanero reaches up to around 350,000 Scoville units.
The ghost pepper measures around 1,000,000 Scoville units and was the first pepper measured over one million.
The Trinidad Moruga Scorpion measures around 1,200,000 Scoville units and features a distinct stinger-like tail.
The Carolina Reaper measures about 1,600,000 Scoville units and held the Guinness World Record for approximately ten years.
Pepper X measures approximately 2,700,000 Scoville units and is currently recognized by Guinness World Records as the hottest pepper in the world.

package.title: Top 5 Funniest Real Sports on Earth
package.description:
Funny, weird sports from around the world that actually exist, with real world championships: extreme ironing, underwater hockey, toe wrestling, bog snorkelling and gurning.

In this Short: 5 funny real sports counted down to the silliest, with when and where each one started.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toe_wrestling
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_hockey
https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/758640-longest-running-gurning-world-championships
package.pinned_comment: Bonus: underwater hockey is also called Octopush in the UK. If you invented a silly sport, what would it be called?

scenes.text: You could become a world champion at one of these five ridiculous sports. All real, counting down to the silliest.
scenes.label: Counting down
scenes.image_prompt: A golden winner's trophy positioned proudly on a rustic table in front of a cheering crowd at an outdoor quirky festival, wide shot, bright sunny day, comedic documentary aesthetic.

scenes.text: Number five: extreme ironing. Ironing clothes on mountains, underwater, anywhere. It started in England in nineteen ninety-seven.
scenes.label: Extreme ironing
scenes.image_prompt: A humorous scene of a hiker in full mountain climbing gear casually pressing a collared shirt on an ironing board atop a jagged rocky mountain peak, crisp daylight, photorealistic.

scenes.text: Number four: underwater hockey. Players with snorkels push a puck along the bottom of a pool. Divers invented it in the nineteen-fifties to stay fit in winter.
scenes.label: Underwater hockey
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater shot of snorkelers swimming along the tiled floor of a clear swimming pool, pushing a miniature puck with small handheld sticks, bubbles rising, cinematic lighting.

scenes.text: Number three: toe wrestling. Two people lock toes and try to pin the other foot down. An English village made it up in the seventies, so England could finally be world champions at something.
scenes.label: Toe wrestling
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up macro shot of two bare feet interlocked by the big toes on a small wooden match frame, intense dramatic sports atmosphere, shallow depth of field.

scenes.text: Number two: bog snorkeling. Two lengths of a muddy trench in Wales, with flippers, and no normal swimming strokes.
scenes.label: Bog snorkeling
scenes.image_prompt: A competitor wearing brightly colored swim goggles, snorkel, and diving flippers propelling through a narrow dark peat bog trench in the countryside, water splashing, humorous action shot.

scenes.text: Number one: gurning. A world championship for pulling the funniest face, at a fair that dates back to twelve sixty-seven.
scenes.label: Gurning
scenes.image_prompt: A close-up shot of a friendly competitor pulling an exaggerated comical distorted face framed through a traditional horse leather collar at a vintage English fair, warm lighting, comic portrait.

package.title: The Cave Found by 4 Teenagers in 1940
package.description:
Who discovered Lascaux? In 1940, four teenagers in France found cave paintings around 17,000 years old. This is the true story of the Lascaux cave discovery, and why the real cave is closed today.

In this Short: Marcel and his dog Robot, the first look at the painted walls, and why visitors now see replicas.

This is a true story.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux
https://www.historytoday.com/node/53687
https://catherinewilsongarry.substack.com/p/four-boys-and-a-dog-called-robot
tags: stone age art lascaux cave paintings
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: one of the most famous images in Lascaux is a huge painted bull more than five meters long. What would you put on a wall for the future?

scenes.text: What would you do if you found a hole in the ground with seventeen-thousand-year-old paintings inside? In nineteen-forty, four teenagers in France actually did. Here's what happened.
scenes.label: 17,000-year-old art?
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of a narrow mysterious hole opening into the ground among tree roots in a lush French woodland forest, soft morning light, 1940 atmosphere, photorealistic documentary style.

scenes.text: It's September, near the village of Montignac. Teenager Marcel finds a hole. The story goes, his dog Robot led him there.
scenes.label: Marcel + his dog Robot
scenes.image_prompt: A 1940s French teenage boy standing with his small dog sniffing around overgrown brush and rocks near a hidden hole in the ground, rural Montignac landscape, cinematic period photography.

scenes.text: Days later, he returns with three friends and a lamp. They squeeze down into the dark.
scenes.label: 3 friends + 1 lamp
scenes.image_prompt: Four teenage boys in 1940s vintage work clothes crawling through a narrow dark limestone cave passage, holding a single glowing vintage oil lamp, dramatic shadows, realistic historical recreation.

scenes.text: The walls are covered in hundreds of painted animals. Horses, bulls, deer, in red, yellow and black. They'd found Lascaux, with paintings around seventeen thousand years old.
scenes.label: Walls full of animals
scenes.image_prompt: Immense natural limestone cave cavern illuminated by warm lamp light, prehistoric Paleolithic cave paintings of running bulls and horses in ochre, charcoal, and red pigments, stunning detail, authentic Lascaux style.

scenes.text: Soon, crowds of visitors came. But all that breath and body heat started damaging the paintings.
scenes.label: Breath + heat = damage
scenes.image_prompt: Mid-20th century crowds of tourists walking inside a dimly lit ancient stone cavern, visible condensation and humidity on ancient painted rock walls, archival documentary aesthetic.

scenes.text: So in nineteen sixty-three, the cave was closed to the public. Today, visitors see exact replicas instead.
scenes.label: Closed in 1963
scenes.image_prompt: Heavy sealed locked iron gate guarding the dark entrance of a historic cave in France, surrounded by dense green forest, dramatic atmospheric lighting, modern documentary look.

scenes.text: Four teens, one lamp, and one of the greatest art discoveries ever. What would you paint for people seventeen thousand years from now? Tell me below. And what would you do if you found a hole in the ground…
scenes.label: What would YOU paint?
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of ancient prehistoric rock art warmly illuminated by a single flickering oil lamp, fading softly into dark limestone textures, contemplative and epic archaeological mood.

key_facts: In September 1940, four teenagers discovered the Lascaux cave near Montignac, France.
Marcel Ravidat initially found the hole, reportedly guided by his dog Robot.
He returned with three friends and a lamp to squeeze inside and explore.
The cave walls were adorned with hundreds of paintings of animals such as horses, bulls, and deer in red, yellow, and black pigments.
The paintings at Lascaux date back approximately 17,000 years.
Carbon dioxide, heat, and humidity from crowds of visitors began damaging the paintings.
Lascaux was permanently closed to the public in 1963 to preserve the artwork.
Modern visitors view exact replicas of the cave instead.
package.script: What would you do if you found a hole in the ground with seventeen-thousand-year-old paintings inside? In nineteen-forty, four teenagers in France actually did. Here's what happened. It's September, near the village of Montignac. Teenager Marcel finds a hole. The story goes, his dog Robot led him there. Days later, he returns with three friends and a lamp. They squeeze down into the dark. The walls are covered in hundreds of painted animals. Horses, bulls, deer, in red, yellow and black. They'd found Lascaux, with paintings around seventeen thousand years old. Soon, crowds of visitors came. But all that breath and body heat started damaging the paintings. So in nineteen sixty-three, the cave was closed to the public. Today, visitors see exact replicas instead. Four teens, one lamp, and one of the greatest art discoveries ever. What would you paint for people seventeen thousand years from now? Tell me below. And what would you do if you found a hole in the ground…

package.title: A Cloud vs 100 Elephants: Which Is Heavier?
package.description:
How much does a cloud weigh? About as much as 100 elephants. Try this 'which weighs more' quiz with 3 tricky questions: a cloud, the weight of a blue whale tongue, and the Eiffel Tower.

In this Short: three 3-second questions, with the surprising answer and the science behind each one.

Sources:

https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/83817-heaviest-tongue
https://interestingengineering.com/culture/the-eiffel-tower-grow-taller-each-summer

scenes.text: Which weighs more, a fluffy cloud or a hundred elephants? You've got three seconds.
scenes.label: 1 Cloud 🆚 100 Elephants
scenes.image_prompt: Split screen comparison showing a massive fluffy white cumulus cloud in a bright blue sky on the left and a large herd of elephants walking across the savannah on the right, high detail cinematic lighting.

scenes.text: Three questions, three seconds each. Say your answer out loud. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Cloud 🆚 100 Elephants?
scenes.image_prompt: Graphic 3D glowing countdown timer showing numbers 3, 2, 1 against a vibrant quiz show background with neon blue and yellow lighting.

scenes.text: It's basically a tie! A typical puffy cloud holds around a million pounds of water. It only floats because all that water is spread out in tiny droplets over a huge space.
scenes.label: Basically a Tie!
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic wide-angle view of a colossal puffy white cumulus cloud floating over a vast green landscape, with glowing visual diagrams showing microscopic water droplets dispersed in the air.

scenes.text: Question two. What weighs more: a blue whale's tongue, or an elephant? Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Whale Tongue 🆚 Elephant?
scenes.image_prompt: Split screen visual with a majestic blue whale gliding through deep blue ocean water on the left side and an enormous African bull elephant standing in golden grass on the right side.

scenes.text: Another tie! A blue whale's tongue can weigh about as much as a whole elephant.
scenes.label: Another Tie!
scenes.image_prompt: Giant blue whale surfacing and breaching in deep turquoise ocean water with water splashing, balanced alongside a large majestic elephant on a conceptual weight balance scale.

scenes.text: Question three. When is the Eiffel Tower taller: in summer or in winter? Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Tower Taller: Summer or Winter?
scenes.image_prompt: Split comparison of an iconic wrought-iron lattice tower standing under bright summer sunshine on one side and frosted with winter snow on the other side.

scenes.text: So: two ties and a growing tower. How many did you get right? Zero, one, two or all three? Tell me in the comments. Okay, next round. Which weighs more, a fluffy cloud or a hundred elephants?

key_facts: A typical cumulus cloud contains about 500,000 kilograms (1 million pounds) of water droplets.

A blue whale's tongue can weigh around 2.7 metric tons (6,000 pounds), which is comparable to the weight of an adult Asian elephant.
Thermal expansion causes the iron in the Eiffel Tower to expand and make the structure up to 15 centimeters taller during hot summer months.

package.title: Top 5 Animals With Built-In Armor
package.description:
Meet five armored animals, from the armadillo and pangolin to the arapaima, the Amazon fish piranhas can't bite through. Here are the top five animals with built-in armor, ranked.

In this Short: armadillos, pangolins, chitons, the iron-shelled scaly-foot snail and the piranha-proof arapaima.

Sources:
https://jacobsschool.ucsd.edu/news/release/2876

https://news.mit.edu/2015/sea-creature-armor-plating-transparent-ceramic-eyes-1119
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the scaly-foot snail even has iron-coated scales on its foot, not just its shell. Which animal surprised you most, the snail or the arapaima?

scenes.text: Before you meet the Amazon fish piranhas can't bite, you need to see the other four armored animals. Here are five animals that grow their own armor.
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic wide shot of a massive arapaima fish swimming through murky green freshwater of the Amazon river, showing textured armor-like scales, dramatic lighting, photorealistic nature documentary style.

scenes.text: Number five, the three-banded armadillo. It's one of only two armadillos that can roll into a complete ball.
scenes.label: Three-banded armadillo
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up shot of a three-banded armadillo curling into a tight, perfect armored sphere on dry dusty soil, detailed shell plates, realistic wildlife photography.

scenes.text: Number four, the pangolin. Its overlapping scales are made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
scenes.label: Pangolin
scenes.image_prompt: Macro detailed view of thick, overlapping keratin scales of a pangolin walking across dry savanna grass, warm sunset light highlighting scale texture, National Geographic style.

scenes.text: Number three, the chiton. This sea mollusk has hundreds of tiny eyes built into its armor.
scenes.label: Chiton
scenes.image_prompt: Macro high-detail photograph of a marine chiton clinging tightly to a wet coastal rock in a tide pool, showing interlocking shell valves with microscopic crystal eye structures.

scenes.text: Number two, the scaly-foot snail. It lives by deep-sea vents, and its shell is coated in iron minerals.
scenes.label: Scaly-foot snail
scenes.image_prompt: Deep-sea hydrothermal vent scene with dark mineral plumes, focusing on a scaly-foot snail with a metallic, black iron-sulfide coated shell resting on volcanic basalt rock, dramatic submersible lighting.

scenes.text: Number one, the arapaima. This giant Amazon fish swims with piranhas, and their teeth can't get through its scales. A hard outer layer sits on a tough, bendy one underneath, so the bite never breaks through.
scenes.label: Arapaima
scenes.image_prompt: Extreme close-up of the thick, iridescent armored scales of a giant arapaima underwater, with a sharp piranha visible blurred in the background, showing complex dual-layer composite scale texture.

scenes.text: That's the fish piranhas can't bite, and engineers study it for armor. Which of these five would you want your phone case made from? Tell me, then meet that Amazon fish again.
scenes.image_prompt: A modern materials laboratory table with bio-inspired flexible composite armor prototypes next to a heavy-duty rugged smartphone case, illuminated under clean studio lighting.

key_facts: Arapaima scales resist piranha bites due to a hard mineralized outer layer over a flexible collagen-fiber inner layer.
The three-banded armadillo is one of only two armadillo species that can roll completely into a sealed ball.
Pangolin scales are composed of keratin, the same protein found in human fingernails.
Chitons possess shell plates embedded with hundreds of microscopic eyes made of aragonite mineral.
The scaly-foot snail inhabits hydrothermal vents and incorporates iron sulfides into its shell armor.
Engineers study arapaima scales to design lightweight, flexible bio-inspired body armor.
package.script: Before you meet the Amazon fish piranhas can't bite, you need to see the other four armored animals. Here are five animals that grow their own armor. Number five, the three-banded armadillo. It's one of only two armadillos that can roll into a complete ball. Number four, the pangolin. Its overlapping scales are made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails. Number three, the chiton. This sea mollusk has hundreds of tiny eyes built into its armor. Number two, the scaly-foot snail. It lives by deep-sea vents, and its shell is coated in iron minerals. Number one, the arapaima. This giant Amazon fish swims with piranhas, and their teeth can't get through its scales. A hard outer layer sits on a tough, bendy one underneath, so the bite never breaks through. That's the fish piranhas can't bite, and engineers study it for armor. Which of these five would you want your phone case made from? Tell me, then meet that Amazon fish again.

scenes.text: Why do you believe lightning never strikes the same place twice? Real or fake? Three weather facts, three seconds each. Call it before I do.
scenes.label: Real or fake?
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of a bright lightning bolt striking a dark city skyline during a thunderstorm

scenes.text: Fact one, lightning never strikes the same place twice. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Fact 1: Never strikes twice?
scenes.image_prompt: Close up of a ticking stopwatch with dark stormy clouds blurred in the background

scenes.text: Fake! Tall, pointy things get hit again and again. The Empire State Building gets struck about twenty-three times a year.
scenes.label: FAKE
scenes.image_prompt: Dramatic slow motion footage of lightning repeatedly striking the tip of a tall skyscraper

scenes.text: Fact two, lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Fact 2: Hotter than the sun?
scenes.image_prompt: Bright lightning flash side by side with a glowing graphic of the sun in deep space

scenes.text: Real! A bolt can heat the air to about fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit. That's around five times hotter than the sun's surface.
scenes.label: REAL: 50,000 F
scenes.image_prompt: Intense plasma activity on the sun's surface transitioning into a blinding lightning flash

scenes.text: Fact three, it can be too cold to snow. Three, two, one.

scenes.text: Fake! It can snow when it's bitterly cold, but cold air holds less water, so you get less snow.
scenes.label: FAKE: drier air
scenes.image_prompt: Fine dry snow blowing across a frozen, icy ground under an overcast winter sky

scenes.text: So there's your answer key: two fakes and one real. How many did you get right, zero, one, two or three? And if you missed fact one, ask yourself again.
scenes.label: Your score?
scenes.image_prompt: A scoreboard graphic floating over stormy clouds with question marks and text

scenes.text: The tower opened for the World's Fair in eighteen eighty-nine. But Gustave Eiffel's deal only let him use the land for twenty years. After that, Paris could take it down.

scenes.text: So Eiffel needed a reason to keep it. His answer? Science. He backed weather and air resistance experiments up there.

key_facts: The Eiffel Tower opened for the World's Fair in 1889.
Gustave Eiffel's deal only let him use the land for 20 years before Paris could take it down.
Eiffel used scientific experiments, weather tests, and air resistance studies to justify keeping the tower.
In 1898, a Morse code radio message was sent from the tower across Paris.
Army radio tests from the top reached farther and farther, turning the tower into a giant antenna.
By 1909, a permanent radio station sat beneath the tower.
In 1910, Eiffel's deal was extended by 70 years because of its utility as a radio antenna.

scenes.text: Nature gave these creatures ridiculous ways to take a nap. Seriously, wait until you see number one.

scenes.text: Number five, sea otters. Otters hold hands while snoozing so currents do not float them away. It is adorable, tactical clinginess.

package.title: Can You Solve These 3 Physics Illusions? 🧠
package.description: Test your brain with three fast-paced physics illusions where rolling objects seem to defy gravity. Can you get all three right before the timer runs out?
package.pinned_comment: Which illusion tricked your brain the hardest? Let me know your score in the comments below!
key_facts: Double cone rolling objects can appear to roll uphill due to the rising angle of the V-shaped tracks lowering its center of gravity.
Water running uphill on special tracks is an illusion created by the sloping frame of the structure relative to the horizontal water level.

scenes.text: Only a few people get all three right, so let us test your brain with three fast-paced physics illusions. Uphill or downhill?
scenes.label: Physics Illusions Quiz
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of a wooden physics track on a table, dramatic lighting, no text, no people.

scenes.text: Q1. Is this wooden ball rolling uphill or downhill? Look closely at the tracks and make your choice. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Rolling Ball Illusion
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of a wooden ball resting on a slanted wooden rail, studio light, no text.

scenes.text: It is actually rolling downhill. Even though the tracks spread apart, the actual center of gravity drops lower the further it goes.
scenes.label: Downhill
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of a double cone rolling along a diverging wooden track, no text.

scenes.text: Q2. Does this heavy steel cylinder roll uphill or downhill on these metal rails? Trust your eyes and decide right now. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Steel Cylinder Trick
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of a steel cylinder on metal rails, sharp focus, no text.

scenes.text: It is going uphill. The rails widen and slope upward, but the cylinder's low center of mass lets it climb against our expectations.
scenes.label: Uphill
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of a metallic roller on an ascending V track, clean background, no text.

scenes.text: Q3. Here is the hardest one. Is this flowing water moving uphill or downhill across the wooden board? Think fast. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Water Flow Puzzle
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of water flowing down a wooden channel, macro shot, no text.

scenes.text: It is rolling downhill. The entire wooden frame is tilted, tricking your brain into thinking the water defies gravity.
scenes.label: Downhill
scenes.image_prompt: Vertical 9:16 image of water moving through a tilted wooden sluice, dramatic contrast, no text.

scenes.text: That was tough. Drop your score in the comments and let us know if...
scenes.label: Comment Your Score

package.description:
These are the longest living animals on Earth, from a tortoise of about 194 to Ming the clam, the oldest animal in the world ever aged at 507 years. Number one is the immortal jellyfish, which can restart its own life.

In this Short: Jonathan the tortoise, the bowhead whale, the Greenland shark, Ming the clam and the immortal jellyfish.

https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/09/science/jonathan-tortoise-longevity-genetics

https://maritime-executive.com/article/greenland-shark-nearly-four-hundred-years-old

package.title: How Mapmakers Invented a Town in 1925
package.description:
Agloe, New York was a fake town on a map, made up by mapmakers as a copyright trap to catch copycats. This is how that paper town ended up becoming real.

In this Short: the 1920s map trap, the fishing lodge that took the name, and how Agloe ended up in a US government database.

This is a true story.

Sources:

package.title: 3-Second Space Quiz: Can You Spot the Myth?
package.description:
Can you spot the myth in this 3-second space quiz? Find out if a day on Venus is longer than its year, if you can see the Great Wall of China from space, and how long Moon footprints last.

In this Short: three space facts, three seconds each, and one myth almost everyone believes.

Sources:
https://www.theweathernetwork.com/en/news/science/space/how-long-is-the-solar-systems-longest-day-venus-has-the-answer
https://www.universetoday.com/25364/can-you-see-the-great-wall-of-china-from-space/
https://www.space.com/35352-eugene-cernan-moon-legacy-footprints.html

why is venus day longer than year
can you see the great wall from space
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: Venus also spins backwards compared to most planets, so the Sun there rises in the west. Which fact did you get wrong?

scenes.text: Before you scroll, can you spot which of these three space facts is fake? Three facts, three seconds each, and one is a myth.
scenes.label: 1 of these is FAKE
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic deep space starfield slowly rotating with Earth visible in the corner, high quality, photorealistic.

scenes.text: Fact one. A day on Venus is longer than its whole year. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Venus: day > year?
scenes.image_prompt: Yellow cloudy planet Venus rotating in the dark void of space, large countdown numbers overlaid, realistic.

scenes.text: True. Venus takes about two hundred forty-three Earth days to spin once, but only about two hundred twenty-five to circle the Sun.
scenes.label: TRUE: 243 vs 225 days
scenes.image_prompt: Animated rocky planet orbiting around a bright Sun with orbital paths visible, scientific visualization style.

scenes.text: Fact two. You can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Great Wall from space?
scenes.image_prompt: The Great Wall of China winding across green mountain ridges under bright daylight, aerial drone view.

scenes.text: Fake. Astronauts say it's too narrow and blends into the land around it.
scenes.label: FAKE: too narrow
scenes.image_prompt: Planet Earth viewed from a space station window with a bold red X graphic overlaid, cinematic lighting.

scenes.text: Fact three. Astronaut footprints on the Moon could last millions of years. Three, two, one.
scenes.label: Moon footprints forever?
scenes.image_prompt: Grey dusty lunar surface under harsh space sunlight with countdown numbers floating in the dark sky.

scenes.text: True. The Moon has no wind or rain to wipe them away.
scenes.label: TRUE: no wind, no rain
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a crisp human boot print pressed into grey lunar dust on the Moon, high detail.

scenes.text: So the fake was the Great Wall, the myth almost everybody grew up believing. Which one fooled you, Venus, the Wall, or the footprints? Tell me, then try the next round before you scroll.
scenes.label: Which one got you?
stock_queries: venus and moon side by side
scenes.image_prompt: Planets Venus, Earth, and the Moon floating side by side in a starfield, cinematic composition, vibrant colors.
scenes.stock_query: venus and moon side by side

key_facts: A day on Venus is longer than its year (243 Earth days to spin once versus 225 to orbit the Sun).
The Great Wall of China cannot be seen from space with the naked eye because it is too narrow.
Astronaut footprints on the Moon can last millions of years due to the lack of wind and rain.
package.script: Before you scroll, can you spot which of these three space facts is fake? Three facts, three seconds each, and one is a myth. Fact one. A day on Venus is longer than its whole year. Three, two, one. True. Venus takes about two hundred forty-three Earth days to spin once, but only about two hundred twenty-five to circle the Sun. Fact two. You can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes. Three, two, one. Fake. Astronauts say it's too narrow and blends into the land around it. Fact three. Astronaut footprints on the Moon could last millions of years. Three, two, one. True. The Moon has no wind or rain to wipe them away. So the fake was the Great Wall, the myth almost everybody grew up believing. Which one fooled you, Venus, the Wall, or the footprints? Tell me, then try the next round before you scroll.

package.title: Why Golf Balls Have 300+ Dimples
package.description:
Why do golf balls have dimples, and how many dimples on a golf ball are there? Most have 300 to 500 golf ball dimples, and they cut drag and add lift so the ball flies about twice as far as a smooth one.

In this Short: how a smooth ball drags, what the dimples do to the air, and why beat-up balls flew farther.

Sources:
https://mentalfloss.com/article/650345/why-golf-balls-have-dimples
https://www.scienceabc.com/sports/golf-balls-dimpled-reason-speed-air-aerodynamic-drag.html
tags: how many dimples on a golf ball
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: some golf balls use hexagon-shaped dimples instead of round ones to cut drag even more. How many dimples do you think your ball has?

package.title: Play-Doh Was Wallpaper Cleaner for 20 Years
package.description:
Play-Doh history in under a minute: Play-Doh was a wallpaper cleaner for about 20 years before it became a toy. Here's who invented Play-Doh as a toy, and the teacher who gave it its second life.

In this Short: coal soot, Kutol's wallpaper cleaner, and how teacher Kay Zufall helped turn it into Play-Doh.

This is a true story.

Sources:
https://www.museumofplay.org/blog/the-history-of-play-doh-good-clean-fun/
https://greatpatent.com/play-doh-was-a-wallpaper-cleaner-dying-with-the-coal-furnace
tags: play doh was originally wallpaper cleaner
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: by 1957, just a couple of years after its toy debut, Play-Doh came in red, yellow and blue. Which color did you always grab first?

scenes.text: It was a wall cleaner for about twenty years. But after World War Two, families switched to oil and gas heat. Less soot, fewer dirty walls, and sales slid.

scenes.text: Then a nursery school teacher named Kay Zufall had her class make crafts with it. She told her brother-in-law, Joe McVicker, who ran the company, to sell it as a toy.
scenes.label: Teacher Kay Zufall
